beats.t: Remi was halfway through his midnight radio show when every phone line in the studio lit up at once.
beats.title: DAY 1 · 11:52 PM

beats.t: Caller after caller, screaming the same thing. People were attacking people, all across the city.
He walked to the window. From sixty-two floors up, he watched the city start to burn.
Then the building alarm went off. The elevators froze. The lights flickered and died.
With a flashlight in his hand, he opened the stairwell door, just a crack.
Far below, something was climbing. Slowly. Floor by floor.
He slammed the door, dragged a filing cabinet in front of it, and didn't sleep at all that night.
In the morning, he took stock of everything he had.
Eighteen bottles of water. One vending machine full of snacks. And forty liters of fuel for the backup generator on the roof.
The vending machine became his pantry. Chips, crackers, and forty-one chocolate bars.
He gave himself three rules. One meal a day. Two bottles of water. And never, ever make noise near the stairs.
The generator burned two liters an hour. That meant twenty hours of power. Total.
Twenty hours. He could use it for light, for heat… or for the radio.
Remi chose the radio. One hour on air every night. No music. Only information.
Which streets were blocked. Where the fires were spreading. Which buildings still had lights on.
From the top of the tower, he could see the whole city. So he started watching it, with an old pair of binoculars.
He wrote down everything. The infected followed noise and light. They hated the cold wind off the river. And they were slowest just after sunrise.
Every night, he read his notes on air… and wondered if anyone out there was even listening.
On the seventh night, the radio crackled back.
A girl's voice. Her name was Tess. She was hiding in a pharmacy with her little brother, twelve blocks away.
Twelve blocks. Through the most crowded streets in the city.
That same night, the scratching started. Something was on his floor, right behind the stairwell door.
He pushed the sofa against the cabinet. The handle rattled until dawn… and then it stopped.
Water was the real problem now. Six bottles left. Maybe four days.
Then, on day ten, a storm rolled in. Remi climbed to the roof with every trash can he could carry.
By morning, he had thirty liters of rainwater. He laughed out loud for the first time in days.
Tess's voice was weaker now. The infected had found the pharmacy door.
Remi studied his map for hours. There was one way out. Along the river, against the wind… at sunrise.
He talked them through it, street by street. Left at the bakery. Stay low past the bus. Don't run. Running is loud.
In the pale morning light, two tiny figures slipped out of the pharmacy.
One of the infected turned its head toward them. Tess froze, exactly like Remi had told her.
Then the wind blew in from the river… and it turned away.
Forty minutes later, they reached the old footbridge. Waiting underneath was a boat full of survivors.
When Tess's voice came back on the radio, Remi sat back in his chair… and cried.
But every broadcast cost fuel. By day fifteen, there were only three liters left. Enough for one last hour.
Then, on the eighteenth evening, he heard it. A low thumping sound, coming from across the river.
A rescue helicopter, flying a search pattern. In the dark, they would never spot one man in a silent tower.
So Remi climbed to the roof with the last of the fuel, and poured every drop into the generator.
He flipped every switch at once. For the first time in eighteen days, the tallest building in the city lit up.
The helicopter turned.
But the light called something else too. Below him, the stairwell filled with noise. Hundreds of them were climbing.
The barricade held for eleven minutes.
That was enough. A rope dropped from the sky, and Remi grabbed it with both hands.
Inside, the pilot handed him a headset. We heard your broadcasts, she said. All of them. There's a whole camp by the river because of you.
And waiting at that camp, holding a little radio, were Tess and her brother.
Remi spent eighteen days in that tower. He never fought a single infected. He survived by watching, thinking… and talking.
